questions.stem: A search must return events where the `clientip` field and the `ipaddress` field hold the same value. Which search does that?

options.text: `index=web | where clientip=ipaddress`
options.explanation: where compares two field values directly. This is the only construct in the list that treats ipaddress as a field rather than as text.

options.text: `index=web clientip=ipaddress`
options.explanation: The search command expects a field compared to a literal, so it looks for events whose clientip is the eight-character string ipaddress. It almost always returns nothing.

options.text: `index=web | search clientip=ipaddress`
options.explanation: Explicitly piping to search changes nothing. search reads the right-hand side as a literal wherever it appears.

options.text: `index=web | eval clientip=ipaddress`
options.explanation: eval assigns rather than filters. This overwrites clientip with the value of ipaddress on every event and removes no events at all.

questions.overallExplanation: Comparing two fields is a where job. search compares a field to a literal value, so a bare field name on the right-hand side is read as a string. The same rule gives the negative form: use `where fieldA!=fieldB`, not a search expression.

guide.blueprintTitle: Use the search and where commands to filter results
guide.verdictNote: The where page states the command is used to compare two different fields, which is the distinction the exam tests most often in this objective.

docs.title: where command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Description: where compares two fields, unlike search which compares a field to a literal.

questions.stem: How does the `search` command evaluate `host="www1" AND status=200 OR action="addtocart"`?

options.text: `host="www1" AND (status=200 OR action="addtocart")`
options.explanation: search evaluates OR before AND, so the OR binds its two neighbours first and the AND applies to the result.

options.text: `(host="www1" AND status=200) OR action="addtocart"`
options.explanation: That is how eval and where read it, because they evaluate AND before OR. search is the exception.

options.text: Strictly left to right, so `((host="www1" AND status=200) OR action="addtocart")`.
options.explanation: SPL applies operator precedence rather than plain left-to-right evaluation, and the result happens to match the eval ordering, not search's.

options.text: It errors, because Boolean operators must be parenthesised in the search command.
options.explanation: Parentheses are recommended for clarity but are not required. The expression runs.

questions.overallExplanation: Precedence differs by command. In search, NOT then OR then AND. In eval and where, NOT then AND then OR. Parenthesise anything that mixes them, which is what the documentation itself recommends.

guide.blueprintTitle: Use the search and where commands to filter results
guide.verdictNote: A second difference worth knowing: search has no XOR operator, while eval and where both do.

docs.title: search command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Usage: operator precedence in the search command places OR ahead of AND.

questions.stem: Some events in an index have no `status` field. Which search returns every event except those whose status is 404, including the events that have no status field at all?

options.text: `index=web NOT status=404`
options.explanation: NOT negates the whole match, so anything that is not an event with status 404 comes back, including events that never had a status field.

options.text: `index=web status!=404`
options.explanation: The != form requires the field to exist with a different value, so every event missing status is silently dropped.

options.text: `index=web | where status!=404`
options.explanation: where evaluates the expression per event and a null status makes the comparison untrue, so those events are dropped here too.

options.text: `index=web | search status!=404 OR status=*`
options.explanation: Both sides require a status field to exist, so the OR still excludes every event without one.

questions.overallExplanation: `field!=value` is a positive test that the field exists and differs. `NOT field=value` is a true negation covering the missing-field case. The corollary is worth memorising: `NOT field=*` returns events where the field is null, while `field!=*` never returns anything.

guide.blueprintTitle: Use the search and where commands to filter results
guide.verdictNote: This is one of the highest-yield facts in section 2.0 because it decides result counts rather than syntax validity.

docs.title: search command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Difference between NOT and != when a field is absent.

questions.stem: Which two statements about case sensitivity in SPL are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: In the search command, field names are case sensitive but field values are not.
options.explanation: `Status=200` will not find a field named status, but `status=OK` matches a stored value of ok.

options.text: Expressions in eval and where are case sensitive.
options.explanation: The eval and where pages both state the expression is case-sensitive, which is why `where status="ok"` and `where status="OK"` behave differently.

options.text: Keyword searches are case sensitive unless wrapped in `TERM()`.
options.explanation: Keyword searches are case-insensitive by default. `CASE()` is the function that makes a term match case-sensitively.

options.text: The `like()` function matches without regard to case.
options.explanation: like() matches case-sensitively, which catches people who expect SQL-style behaviour.

questions.overallExplanation: There is no single rule. Under search, field names are case sensitive, values are not, and keywords are insensitive unless wrapped in CASE(). Under eval and where, everything is case sensitive, including like().

guide.blueprintTitle: Use the search and where commands to filter results
guide.verdictNote: Splunk's own study material contradicts itself on this point, which is why the exam can afford to ask it. Answer from the search and eval pages rather than from memory of a course slide.

docs.title: Comparison and Conditional functions (SPL Search Reference 10.4)

options.text: It takes one or more arguments and returns the first value that is not NULL.
options.explanation: That is the documented behaviour. It is the standard way to merge several source-specific field names into one.

options.text: It takes a predicate and returns the second argument when the predicate is true.
options.explanation: That describes if(), which takes exactly three arguments: a predicate, a true value and a false value.

options.text: It takes two fields and returns NULL when they are equal.
options.explanation: That is nullif(). coalesce does not compare its arguments to each other.

options.text: It takes no arguments and returns NULL, clearing a field when assigned.
options.explanation: That is null(). Assigning it is how you clear a field value in eval.

questions.overallExplanation: Four functions that get swapped for each other on exams: coalesce() returns the first non-null of its arguments, if() is the three-argument conditional, nullif() returns NULL when two fields are equal, and null() takes no arguments at all.

guide.verdictNote: The printed Apress study guide states the coalesce and null definitions incorrectly in its Table 2-16, which is recorded in source-notes/apress-errata.md. Answer from the docs.

docs.title: Comparison and Conditional functions (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: coalesce(<values>) returns the first value that is not null.

questions.stem: What happens when a value matches none of the conditions in a `case()` expression?

options.text: The expression returns NULL.
options.explanation: case() returns NULL when no condition evaluates to TRUE. The documented idiom for a default is a final `true(), "<default>"` pair.

options.text: The last value listed is returned as a fallback.
options.explanation: There is no implicit fallback. Nothing about being last makes a value a default.

options.text: The original field value is left unchanged.
options.explanation: The assignment still happens; the field is set to NULL rather than left alone.

options.text: The search errors at the first event with no matching condition.
options.explanation: No error is raised. A NULL result is normal and simply means no branch matched.

questions.overallExplanation: case() needs an explicit default: end it with `true(), "<default>"`. Its mirror is validate(), which returns the value for the first condition that is FALSE and defaults to NULL when every condition is TRUE.

guide.verdictNote: Knowing validate() as case()'s mirror is worth a mark on its own, since it is the less familiar of the pair and appears in distractors.

docs.title: Comparison and Conditional functions (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: case() returns NULL if none of the conditions are true; validate() is documented as its opposite.

questions.stem: Why does `... | eval matched = isnull(user)` fail?

options.text: The result of an eval expression cannot be a Boolean.
options.explanation: isnull() returns a Boolean, and eval cannot assign one to a field. Wrap it in if(), case() or validate(), or convert it with tostring().

options.text: isnull() is a where-only function and is not available to eval.
options.explanation: isnull() is available to eval. The problem is what it returns, not where it lives.

options.text: matched is a reserved field name in Splunk.
options.explanation: There is no such reservation. Any name that is not an existing field simply creates a new one.

options.text: isnull() takes two arguments, so the call is incomplete.
options.explanation: isnull() takes a single field. The call itself is well formed.

questions.overallExplanation: The same restriction hits in(), like(), cidrmatch(), searchmatch() and the whole is* family under eval. Under where they are used directly, because where wants a Boolean. `eval matched = if(isnull(user), "yes", "no")` is the working form.

guide.verdictNote: The eval Usage section states that booleans cannot be assigned to fields, which is the single sentence this whole family of questions rests on.

docs.title: eval command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Usage: an eval expression cannot return a Boolean value.

questions.stem: A results table has null cells in several columns. What does a bare `| fillnull` do?

options.text: Writes 0 into every null cell of every field.
options.explanation: The default value is 0, and with no field list the command applies to all fields in the result set.

options.text: Writes the string NULL into every null cell of every field.
options.explanation: NULL is not the default. Getting a NULL string requires `fillnull value=NULL`.

options.text: Writes an empty string into every null cell of every field.
options.explanation: An empty string is a common guess but is not documented as the default.

options.text: Copies the last non-null value from the row above.
options.explanation: That is filldown. fillnull writes one constant everywhere; filldown carries a value forward.

questions.overallExplanation: Two commands, two behaviours. fillnull writes a constant, defaulting to 0, and takes a plain field list with no wildcard support. filldown copies the last non-null value seen above and takes a wildcard field list.

guide.verdictNote: In the syntax, `value=` precedes the field list. Writing the field list first is a common way to get a confusing error.

docs.title: fillnull command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Default value is 0; with no field list it applies to all fields.

questions.stem: A search ends with `| fieldformat bytes=tostring(bytes,"commas") | sort - bytes | outputcsv report`. What is written to the CSV?

options.text: The original numeric values, sorted numerically.
options.explanation: fieldformat changes rendering only. Both sort and outputcsv see the underlying numeric value, so the sort is numeric and the file holds raw numbers.

options.text: The comma-formatted strings, sorted numerically.
options.explanation: Export commands do not see the formatted value at all, so the commas never reach the file.

options.text: The comma-formatted strings, sorted lexicographically.
options.explanation: This would be true if fieldformat changed the value, but it does not, so neither half happens.

options.text: The original numeric values, sorted lexicographically.
options.explanation: The values stay numeric, so sort orders them numerically rather than as text.

questions.overallExplanation: fieldformat is display-only and is invisible to every later command, including outputcsv and outputlookup. Use eval when the change has to persist, and put fieldformat last in the pipeline. It also takes one expression per command.

guide.verdictNote: tostring() accepts only binary, hex, commas and duration. commas rounds to two decimal places, and there is no currency option, so a symbol has to be concatenated.

docs.title: fieldformat command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Changes the display of a field without changing its underlying value; export commands see the original.

docs.title: Conversion functions (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: tostring() format options are binary, hex, commas and duration.
